question: Which statement best describes The global scope problem?
options: Every CSS rule lives in one global namespace. A selector like .button written by one team applies everywhere .button appears, so two features can silently style each other. As a codebase grows, this leads to fear of editing existing CSS, dead styles nobody dares delete, and bugs from collisions. Architecture exists primarily to re-introduce boundaries CSS doesn't give you natively.

BEM (Block__Element--Modifier) is a naming convention that encodes structure into class names so selectors stay single-class and flat: a Block is a component (.card), an Element is a part of it (.card__title), and a Modifier is a variant (.card--featured). It trades verbose class names for near-zero specificity conflicts and self-documenting markup, all in plain CSS with no build step.

Utility-first CSS provides tiny single-purpose classes (.flex, .p-4, .text-center) that you compose directly in markup, so you rarely write new CSS or invent names. Tailwind is the popular implementation, generating utilities from a design-token config and purging unused ones at build time. It eliminates naming and dead-CSS problems and keeps the stylesheet bounded, at the cost of verbose class lists in HTML.

When styles collide, the cascade resolves them by specificity. Teams escalate selectors (.nav .list li a) or add !important to win, which forces the next person to escalate further — a 'specificity war' that ratchets stylesheets toward unmaintainable. Good architecture keeps specificity flat and predictable so order, not selector weight, decides the winner.
